headline: SMSF limited recourse borrowing arrangements for residential property banned under new legislation, affecting ~$77bn or 7% of total SMSF assets
reasoning: The Australian government passed legislation banning SMSFs from using limited recourse borrowing arrangements (LRBAs) for residential property, effective 45 days after royal assent. Existing arrangements are grandfathered but no new residential property borrowing via SMSF will be permitted. LRBAs represent the fifth-largest asset class within SMSFs, having grown from zero in 2010 to over 7% of total SMSF assets (~$77bn). Commercial property and business real property appear unaffected. The SMSF Association is lobbying for a carve-out to allow new residential builds, which could still benefit Australia's housing supply needs. SMSFs can still invest in residential property without leverage if they have sufficient assets.
quote: So as I said, it's gone from a sort of a standing start of 0 in 2010 to sort of. Yeah, north of, north of um, 7% of all our, um, super fund SMSF assets. So it's the fifth largest asset class, so to speak... What happened with the passage last week of the bill is that going forward, I think it's technically 45 days after the bill becomes law receives royal assent. Um, SMSF trustees won't be able to use those limited recourse borrowing arrangements for residential property. So once again, let's be clear here. Grandfathered. So if you're in you're in. But if you're thinking of getting into the residential investing property market through your SMSF, um, that won't be allowed.
episode_title: $77 billion of SMSF assets caught in the crosshairs | the advisory

headline: Direct shares (Australian and overseas) and cash/term deposits dominate SMSF asset allocation, collectively representing ~44% of total SMSF assets
reasoning: Harry Chemay highlighted that the two largest asset classes within SMSFs are direct shares (both Australian and overseas), accounting for approximately 27% of assets, followed by cash and term deposits at around 17%. This means roughly four to four-and-a-half dollars in every ten held in an SMSF is concentrated in these two categories. Unit trusts (managed funds) are the third-largest category, followed by commercial property, with residential property LRBAs in fifth place.

headline: SMSF trustees must weigh falling residential property values against prospective yields when deciding whether to invest in residential property without leverage
reasoning: Following the ban on LRBAs for residential property, SMSF trustees who wish to invest in residential property must do so without borrowing, requiring sufficient existing assets within the fund. Harry Chemay notes that property values are currently falling, adding complexity to the decision. Each trustee must individually assess prospective yields and returns from residential property versus commercial property as an asset class. The broader negative gearing changes form part of the same policy package in which this SMSF measure is embedded.

Of course, what we're seeing in the property market at the moment. Values are falling. That's the thing, right? So every every SMSF trustee will have to make their own decisions... How they see prospective yields and returns on Australian property, residential property as an asset class versus a commercial property. Each trustee will have to make their own mind up about that.
